facts.fact: Described in 2014 by Keith, Hadiaty, Busson and Hubert in the journal Cybium (38(3): 173–178).
It is a sicydiine goby in the amphidromous genus Sicyopus.
The species name rubicundus refers to its bright red throat and belly.
The genus name Sicyopus comes from Greek words meaning 'cucumber' and 'foot'.
Both sexes have five spines in the first dorsal fin. The second dorsal and anal fins each have one spine and nine segmented rays.
It has 10–12 scales in a zigzag series, compared with 7–9 in other Sicyopus species.
Its caudal peduncle is deeper (10–12% of SL) and its fins are longer than in other Sicyopus species.
Unlike S. zosterophorum, it has no black stripe under the eye and no clearly visible vertical stripes, and its base colour is more orange than red.
Sicyopus auxilimentus differs from it by lacking orange lips.
The holotype is MZB 22123, from Kabupaten Pandeglang, Banten, Java.
It has not been evaluated for the IUCN Red List.
Aquarium Glaser imported it in 2006 under the working name Sicyopus sp. Red, years before it was described.
It is native to Indonesia and was described from Java and Bali.
Before 2025 it had been recorded only from Java, Lombok and Bali.
In 2024 it was collected on Nias Island, North Sumatra, in the Humogo River (a tributary of the Idanoi River, Gunungsitoli City) and the Nalua River (Nias Utara District).
The 2025 Sumatra records are a significant range extension within Indonesia.
It was collected in small, fast, boulder-strewn mountain streams with rocky bottoms.
It was collected at altitudes of 100–500 m above sea level.
It is a freshwater, bottom-dwelling, tropical fish.
It is rare in the aquarium trade and is sold as the Red Lipstick Goby.
Newly imported fish may refuse dry and frozen foods, and the video's keepers lost almost half their group before the fish accepted them.
It is a poor choice for tanks where cherry shrimp or livebearers are meant to breed.
Imported fish may look colourless at first, and males colour up later.
It prefers clear, clean, flowing water.
Give it hiding places and a sandy bottom.
It is a micro-predator that chases anything small enough to swallow, including shrimp and livebearer fry.
It has been seen eating fully grown cherry shrimp.
Unlike Stiphodon and Sicyopterus, it does not graze on algae or biofilm. It takes fairly large prey, including very small fish and shrimp up to about 1 cm.
Once settled it can be weaned onto flakes, granules and frozen foods. Newly imported fish may also refuse microworms.
Subordinate males show duller colours than the dominant male, possibly to avoid provoking it.
In the video's tank, endler fry were never seen again until the gobies were moved out.
Mature males have orange-red lips, and the same colour runs along the rear half of the body toward the tail fin.
Females are much duller in colour than males.
Males are orange overall with bright orange lips, while females are almost colourless.
Males have a distinctive body colour, which is one of the features used to tell the species apart.
In aquaria it spawns regularly as a cave brooder.
Its larvae are tiny and need marine conditions to develop, and no successful rearing in the hobby has been reported.
Aquarium spawnings have been reported, but raising the fry is very difficult because of their complex larval stages.
The genus is amphidromous: its larvae develop at sea before returning to fresh water.
